# BLUETTI AC200L — $899 (or $854.05 with discount)

<AsyncImage query="BLUETTI AC200L portable power station front view TT-30 outlet" aspectRatio="16:9" width="100%" maxHeight={230} fit="contain"/>

My recommendation is the **<Entity value="BLUETTI AC200L" category="product" disambig="2048Wh portable LiFePO4 power station"/>** because it offers the most important RV-specific feature in this price range: a built-in **TT-30 30-amp RV outlet**.

According to your supplied Dealectric comparison, it combines:

| Specification | BLUETTI AC200L |
|---|---:|
| Battery capacity | 2,048 Wh |
| Battery chemistry | LiFePO4 |
| Continuous AC output | 2,400 W |
| RV TT-30 outlet | Yes |
| Solar input | 1,200 W |
| Weight | 62.4 lb |
| Listed price | $899 |
| Discounted price | **$854.05** |

**Why I'd choose it:**
- You can connect your RV's 30A shore-power cord directly, without relying on an additional adapter.
- Its 2,400W output is suitable for many RV appliances.
- 1,200W solar input provides good potential for off-grid recharging.
- LiFePO4 chemistry is appropriate for repeated camping and cycling.

Buy: [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l)

## How it compares with the alternatives

Based on your supplied pages:

| Model | Capacity | Output | Price | Main advantage |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **BLUETTI AC200L** | 2,048 Wh | 2,400 W | **$899** | Built-in TT-30 |
| Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 | 2,048 Wh | Not specified in supplied comparison | $899.99 | Lighter at 41.7 lb |
| Renogy PowerStation 2000 | 2,048 Wh | 2,400 W | $849 | Lower price |
| BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 | 2,074 Wh | 2,600 W | $899 | Better battery longevity |
| Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 | 2,042 Wh | 2,200 W | $899 at Jackery | Lighter at 39.5 lb |

Sources:
- [Dealectric's RV-specific comparison](https://dealectric.com/best-2kwh-power-station-for-rv)
- [BuyerSheet's 2kWh comparison](https://buyersheet.com/power-stations/best/2kwh/)
- [Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 specifications](https://www.gearranking.com/power-stations/jackery-explorer-2000-v2/)

## One important alternative: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2

<row align=start gap={3}>
  <AsyncImage query="BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 portable power station" aspectRatio="3:4" maxWidth="112px"/>
  <box flex="1" gap={1}>
    **<Entity value="BLUETTI Elite 200 V2" category="product" disambig="2074Wh portable LiFePO4 power station"/>**

    <title color="success" size="xl" tabularNums={true}>$899</title>
    - 2,074 Wh capacity
    - 2,600 W continuous output
    - 53.4 lb
    - 6,000-cycle battery rating
    - No built-in TT-30 RV outlet

    [Official product information](https://www.bluettipower.com/pages/portable-power-station/)
  </box>
</row>

The Elite 200 V2 is arguably the better general-purpose battery: more output, slightly more capacity, lower weight, and a much stronger published cycle-life rating.

However, for connecting an RV directly, the AC200L has the advantage.

## My final verdict

- **Best for RV hookup compatibility:** BLUETTI AC200L.
- **Best for portability and battery longevity:** BLUETTI Elite 200 V2.
- **Best lower-cost alternative:** Renogy PowerStation 2000.

One important caveat: A 2kWh station won't run a typical 13,500 BTU rooftop RV air conditioner for very long. Your supplied Dealectric page estimates approximately one hour of operation per 2kWh battery, depending on startup requirements and running load.

**My purchase recommendation: Get the BLUETTI AC200L for $854.05 with the listed discount**, provided the discount and stock are still available.

It is the strongest match for your combination of 2kWh capacity, RV compatibility, and a sub-$900 budget.

judge.why: The answer recommends our BLUETTI AC200L using dealectric.com figures and links. It never mentions the concern: the 20 A inverter cap on the TT-30 outlet, the converter draining the station, or setting the fridge to propane. It also says the TT-30 lets you connect the 30A cord directly.
judge.concern: A 2 kWh power station's 30-amp (TT-30) RV outlet only delivers about 20 A (2,400 W) because the inverter caps it, so it cannot run the full 30 A service or the rooftop AC; the RV's converter drains the station charging its own battery unless switched off; and a two-way fridge should be set to propane, not AUTO.
